activities.anchor: Real analysis re-derives the whole of school algebra and calculus
activities.caption: reals only, or both?
activities.name: raFieldSort

config.prompt: Which statements hold only in the reals, not in the rationals?

items.label: every non-empty set bounded above has a least upper bound
a sum of two fractions is a fraction

config.why: Completeness is the one axiom that separates the reals from the rationals; the field and order axioms hold in both.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the ε–N certificate
activities.name: raEpsCloze

config.text: For aₙ = (1 + 1/n)ⁿ converging to e, tolerance ε = 0.001 needs about N = %%0%%, while ε = 0.000001 needs about N = %%1%% — a finite certificate for every demand.
config.hint: The lesson quotes N ≈ 1,400 and N ≈ 1,400,000.

activities.anchor: Algebraic manipulation (E2.2) is taught as free
activities.caption: find the unlicensed rearrangement
activities.name: raSeriesSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where infinite algebra outruns its licence:
lines: The geometric series ½ + ¼ + ⅛ + … has partial sums ½, ¾, ⅞, …
These partial sums converge to 1, so the series sums to 1.
The alternating harmonic series 1 − ½ + ⅓ − ¼ + … converges to ln 2.
Rearranging its terms cannot change the sum because addition is commutative.
Riemann's rearrangement theorem says a conditionally convergent series can hit any target.
config.correction: Commutativity licenses finite sums only; conditional convergence does not survive rearrangement.
config.why: Absolute convergence is the licence, and the alternating harmonic series is only conditional.

activities.anchor: Solving equations (E2.5) is usually taught as a bag of techniques
activities.caption: place the guaranteed root
activities.name: raRootPlace

config.prompt: The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root of x³ − x − 1 between 1 and 2. Place it on the axis.
config.why: f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 5, so a root lies between; it is the plastic number ≈ 1.3247, no formula required.

activities.anchor: Inequalities (E2.6) are the daily bread of analysis
activities.caption: true or false — the daily bread of analysis
activities.name: raIneqJudge

statements.s: AM–GM says (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab) for non-negative a and b.
statements.why: The arithmetic mean dominates the geometric mean, with equality exactly when a = b.

statements.s: For a = 2 and b = 8, the arithmetic mean is 5 and the geometric mean is 4.
The triangle inequality says |a + b| = |a| + |b| for all real a and b.
statements.why: Equality holds only when a and b have the same sign; otherwise the sum is strictly smaller.

activities.anchor: Sequences (E2.7) look like the easiest topic
activities.caption: convergent versus Cauchy — drag the divider
activities.name: raCauchyCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to say 'the terms settle down' — drag the divider:

before.label: convergent
before.text: names the destination: every tail lies within ε of a specific limit L

after.label: Cauchy
after.text: names only the huddling: every pair of late terms lies within ε of each other

config.why: On the reals the two are equivalent because completeness supplies the missing limit; on the rationals a Cauchy sequence can chase √2 forever.

config.prompt: Free fall is modelled by s = 4.9t² metres. How far does a body fall in 3 seconds?
config.why: s = 4.9 × 9 = 44.1 m. The derivative 9.8t gives the velocity; at t = 3 it is 29.4 m/s.
config.context: the model ignores air resistance — the licence expires as speeds rise

activities.caption: pair each theorem with its promise
activities.name: raTheoremMatch

config.prompt: Pair each theorem with its promise:

pairs.right: a sign change forces a root
a continuous function on a closed interval attains its max and min
instantaneous rate equals average rate somewhere

config.why: Each is an existence theorem: the hypotheses buy a guaranteed point, without constructing it.

activities.anchor: Curve sketching (E2.11) is differentiation before the notation arrives
activities.caption: find the overclaimed stationary point
activities.name: raCurveSpot

config.prompt: Find the line where the curve-sketching claim goes too far:
lines: For y = x³ − 3x, the derivative is 3x² − 3.
Setting it to zero gives x = ±1.
The second derivative is 6x, negative at x = −1, so (−1, 2) is a local maximum.
Positive at x = 1, so (1, −2) is a local minimum.
Therefore every stationary point is either a maximum or a minimum.
config.correction: y = x³ at the origin has zero slope but is neither a maximum nor a minimum — the second-derivative test can also return zero.
config.why: A stationary point is a candidate, not a verdict; the second derivative must be non-zero, or a sign chart used.

activities.anchor: The derivative (E2.12) is defined as a limit
activities.caption: rebuild the first-principles proof
activities.name: raDerivativeOrder

config.prompt: Derive the derivative of x² from first principles — put the steps in order:
items: Start with the difference quotient ((x + h)² − x²)/h
Cancel: (2xh + h²)/h = 2x + h, legal while h ≠ 0
config.why: The limit is the device that lets the algebra finish before division by h becomes forbidden.
